title: Measure Preserving Transformations and Poincare Recurrence

items.title: Measure-preserving transformations and systems
items.statement: A measurable map T:X→X preserves μ when μ(T^-1 E)=μ(E) for every measurable E. A system is (X,A,μ,T). A probability system has μ(X)=1.
items.strategy: Use inverse images throughout; no assumption of invertibility or completeness.

items.title: Invertible measure-preserving systems
items.statement: An invertible system has a bijective T with measurable inverse. Invertibility modulo null sets means this holds on an invariant conull measurable restriction.
items.strategy: Distinguish actual bijection from invertibility modulo null sets and from measure preservation.

items.title: Measure preservation can be checked on a generating pi-system
items.statement: Let T be measurable and P generate A as a pi-system. Suppose P has increasing P_n covering X with μ(P_n)<∞ and μ(T^-1 P)=μ(P) for P in P. Then T preserves μ.
items.strategy: Define ν(E)=μ(T^-1 E); inverse images preserve disjoint unions, so ν is a measure. Apply the exact published uniqueness theorem. For finite measures add X to P.

references.title: E–W §2.1 p.13; local sigma-finite uniqueness theorem

items.title: Compositions, iterates and completions preserve invariance
items.statement: Compositions and nonnegative iterates of measure-preserving maps preserve measure. A Borel measure-preserving self-map extends as a measurable preserving map for the completed sigma-algebra.
items.strategy: Pull back identities; for completion sandwich a completed measurable set between a Borel set and a Borel null set, whose preimage is null.

references.title: E–W §2.1, Exercise 2.1.3; Sarig Proposition 1.4 completion argument

items.title: Integral invariance under measure-preserving maps
items.statement: For measurable f≥0, ∫f∘T=∫f in [0,∞]; for integrable real or complex f the same identity holds and f∘T is integrable. Conversely indicator integral invariance implies measure preservation.
items.strategy: Indicators, finite nonnegative simple functions, monotone convergence, then positive/negative and real/imaginary parts.

items.title: The Koopman operator
items.statement: For 1≤p≤∞ set U_T[f]=[f∘T].
items.strategy: Pullbacks of null measurable sets are null; therefore the expression is independent of representatives.

items.title: Koopman operators are linear isometries
items.statement: For 1≤p≤∞, U_T is a well-defined linear isometry. It is onto for an invertible system.
items.strategy: For finite p use ∫|f∘T|^p=∫|f|^p; at infinity compare all superlevel null sets in both directions. Inverse composition provides surjectivity when applicable.

items.title: Strict and mod-null invariant sigma-algebras
items.strategy: Both families contain only measurable sets. Do not assert they always differ: identity makes them equal.

items.title: Both invariant families are sigma-algebras
items.statement: I and I′ are sigma-algebras and I⊆I′.
items.strategy: Complement commutes with pullback; symmetric difference for a countable union is contained in the union of component symmetric differences.

items.title: Mod-null invariant sets have strict representatives
items.statement: For E∈I′ the set F=limsup_n T^-n E lies in I and μ(E Δ F)=0.
items.strategy: Each E Δ T^-n E is null by telescoping; the countable union contains E Δ F. Dropping the first term of a limsup proves exact invariance. No completeness needed.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.14 pp.23–24; Sarig Proposition 1.1 pp.5–6

items.title: Ergodicity relative to an invariant measure
items.statement: T is ergodic for μ if each E∈I has μ(E)=0 or μ(X\E)=0. On a probability space this means measure zero or one.
items.strategy: Name the measure. Permit general measures in the definition, but state subsequent probability hypotheses explicitly.

items.title: Equivalent invariant-set and invariant-function criteria for ergodicity
items.statement: On a probability space ergodicity is equivalent to null/conull mod-null invariant sets, to every invariant measurable real or complex function being constant a.e., and to every f with f∘T=f a.e. being constant a.e.
items.strategy: For a.e. invariant f use rational level sets, countable unions and separation of two distinct real values. For exact invariant functions use indicator of a strict invariant set; the bridge supplies equivalence.

items.title: Positive sets sweep out ergodic probability systems
items.statement: In an ergodic probability system, E of positive measure has μ(union_{n≥1}T^-n E)=1. Equivalently every pair A,B of positive measure has μ(B∩T^-n A)>0 for some n≥1.
items.strategy: The union pulls back into itself with equal finite measure, so is mod-null invariant. Use countable subadditivity and the complement of an invariant set for the converses.

items.title: Strong and weak mixing on a probability space
items.statement: Strong mixing means μ(A∩T^-n B)→μ(A)μ(B) for every A,B. Weak mixing means N^-1 sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|μ(A∩T^-n B)-μ(A)μ(B)|→0.
items.strategy: Absolute values occur inside the Cesaro sum. These definitions use probability normalization.

items.title: Mixing implies weak mixing, which implies ergodicity
items.statement: Every strongly mixing probability system is weakly mixing; every weakly mixing probability system is ergodic.
items.strategy: Split Cesaro averages into a finite initial segment and small tail; apply weak mixing to a strict invariant set against itself.

items.title: Approximation in symmetric difference by a generating algebra
items.statement: If μ(X)<∞ and an algebra C generates A, every E∈A can be approximated in μ(E Δ C) by C∈C.
items.strategy: The approximable sets form a sigma-algebra: complements preserve error and a countable union is first truncated using finite measure, then each of its finitely many terms is approximated.

items.title: Mixing is checkable on a generating pi-system
items.statement: For a measure-preserving probability system, correlations on a generating pi-system containing X suffice to check strong or weak mixing.
items.strategy: Extend to its finite Boolean algebra by finite inclusion-exclusion, then approximate both sets. The error is bounded uniformly in n by twice the sum of their symmetric-difference errors.

references.title: E–W Exercise 2.7.3 pp.52–53 (pi-system extension by finite Boolean algebra)

items.title: Mixing correlations extend to L2 functions
items.statement: Strong or weak mixing is equivalently tested on complex L2 correlations, using conjugation in the second factor.
items.strategy: Approximate by bounded simple functions obtained by truncation and quantization; Cauchy–Schwarz makes the approximation error uniform in n. Indicator functions prove the reverse.

items.title: No-return sets have disjoint null preimage towers
items.statement: If μ(X)<∞ and W=E\ union_{n≥1}T^-n E, then T^-n W, n≥0, are pairwise disjoint and μ(W)=0.
items.strategy: If x belongs to preimages at i<j, T^i x∈W returns to E at time j-i, contradiction. N equal masses are bounded by μ(X).

items.title: Poincare recurrence for finite measure-preserving systems
items.statement: For μ(X)<∞ and E measurable, almost every x∈E returns to E infinitely often at positive integer times.
items.strategy: Every finite-return point eventually enters W at its last visit; hence the exceptional set is contained in union_{n≥0}T^-n W. This also includes points with no positive return.

items.title: Topological recurrence on second-countable spaces
items.statement: Let X have a countable open base contained in A and T preserve a finite measure. Outside a measurable null set, every neighborhood of x is revisited infinitely often. In a metric space there are n_j→∞ with T^{n_j}x→x.
items.strategy: Apply recurrence separately to every basis set, take the countable union of exceptional sets, and then choose the least succeeding time into a shrinking ball.

items.title: First-return times and induced transformations
items.statement: Assume μ(X)<∞. For E measurable of positive measure define r_E(x)=min{n≥1:T^n x∈E}, min empty=∞. On E∞=E∩limsup T^-n E put T_E(x)=T^{r_E(x)}x and μ_E=μ|E∞/μ(E).
items.strategy: Use the infinitely-returning core, not merely the first-return domain: it is conull in E and is mapped into itself.

items.title: First-return time and induced map are measurable
items.statement: r_E is measurable on E and T_E is measurable on E∞ with its trace sigma-algebra.
items.strategy: The level r_E=n is E∩T^-n E∩intersection_{1≤j<n}T^-j(E^c). On each level T_E=T^n; take countable unions of preimages.

items.title: Induced transformations preserve restricted finite measure
items.statement: For a finite measure-preserving system and μ(E)>0, T_E preserves μ|E∞ and μ_E; invertibility and ergodicity are not required.
items.strategy: For B⊆E∞ expand μ(B) by pulling back and splitting at E for N steps. The sum of first-return contributions is ≤μ(B). Apply the same inequality to E∞\B and use T_E^-1 E∞=E∞ to obtain equality.

items.title: Inducing an ergodic system gives an ergodic system
items.statement: If T is ergodic on a probability space and μ(E)>0, then T_E is ergodic for μ_E.
items.strategy: Extend a bounded T_E-invariant function along first entrance into E∞; sweep-out makes this defined a.e.; the extension is T-invariant, hence constant.

items.title: Kac return-time formula without invertibility
items.statement: For an ergodic probability-preserving T and μ(E)>0, ∫_E r_E dμ=1; equivalently ∫r_E dμ_E=1/μ(E).
items.strategy: Let C_N=intersection_{j=0}^{N-1}T^-j(E^c). Pullback invariance gives μ(E∩{r_E>j})=μ(C_j)-μ(C_{j+1}), with C_0=X. Sum j<N, use sweep-out for μ(C_N)→0, then monotone convergence of tail sums.

items.title: Kac integral formula for excursions
items.statement: In the same ergodic probability setting, ∫f dμ=∫_E sum_{j=0}^{r_E-1}f(T^j x)dμ for nonnegative measurable f and for integrable real/complex f.
items.strategy: Repeatedly split the integral into E and E^c after pullback. For bounded nonnegative f the remainder is ≤||f||∞ times the measure of avoiding E for N steps. Truncate and use monotone convergence; apply first to |f| before signed decomposition.

items.title: The circle, rotations and the doubling map
items.statement: Use [0,1) with d(x,y)=min(|x-y|,1-|x-y|), Borel or completed Lebesgue measure λ, Rα(x)={x+α}, and D(x)={2x}.
items.strategy: Check the circle metric and countable arc base; distinguish it from the ordinary interval topology. Both maps are continuous in the circle metric.

items.title: Circle rotations preserve Lebesgue measure
items.statement: Rα is an invertible λ-preserving circle map for every real α.
items.strategy: Split a wrapping interval at the endpoint, use translation invariance and the finite pi-system criterion, then completion.

items.title: Irrational circle orbits are dense
items.statement: If α is irrational then {nα mod 1:n∈Z} is dense. There are arbitrarily large positive n with d(nα,0) arbitrarily small.
items.strategy: Pigeonhole two of 0,α,...,Nα into the same one of N arcs. The nonzero difference is arbitrarily close to an integer; multiples give a fine net. Unboundedness follows because no fixed nonzero multiple is an integer.

references.title: E–W Proposition 2.16 p.26 and Example 2.33 p.49

items.title: Circle rotation is ergodic for Lebesgue measure exactly at irrational angles
items.statement: Assume countable choice. Rα on the Lebesgue circle is ergodic iff α is irrational.
items.strategy: Rational case: finite union of short translates. Irrational case: take density points of an invariant set and its complement; choose a common small radius with both density ratios >0.9, and rotate the first center within radius/10 of the second using orbit density. The translated almost-full interval must overlap the other almost-full interval in positive measure, contradiction.

items.title: Doubling preserves Lebesgue measure
items.statement: D is a non-injective λ-preserving map on the circle.
items.strategy: The preimage of [a,b) is [a/2,b/2) disjoint union [(a+1)/2,(b+1)/2); use the generator criterion and completion.

items.title: Doubling is ergodic for Lebesgue measure
items.statement: Assume countable choice. D is ergodic for λ.
items.strategy: For a strict invariant A and every generation-n dyadic interval I, branch D^n maps I linearly onto [0,1), giving λ(A∩I)=λ(A)λ(I). A density point of A has dyadic density tending to one: I is contained in a centered interval of twice its length. Hence λ(A)=1 if positive.

references.title: Sarig Proposition 1.5 p.9, conclusion; density argument is the MT-22 prescribed local replacement

items.title: Doubling is strongly mixing for Lebesgue measure
items.statement: Doubling is strongly mixing for λ.
items.strategy: For dyadic intervals of depths r,s and n≥r, direct branch counting gives λ(I∩D^-n J)=λ(I)λ(J). Apply the generator criterion.

items.title: Binary-sequence cylinders and fair-coin content
items.statement: On Ω={0,1}^{N_0}, prescribe finitely many coordinates; give a cylinder fixing k coordinates mass 2^-k, and finite disjoint unions the sum.
items.strategy: Use the algebra of finite unions of cylinders, not the collection of cylinders alone. Common refinement proves the content is well-defined and finitely additive.

items.title: Binary-sequence space is compact without Tychonoff
items.statement: The metric d(x,y)=2^-min{j:x_j≠y_j}, d(x,x)=0, has the cylinder topology and is compact in ZF.
items.strategy: If an open cover has no finite subcover, choose recursively the first binary child cylinder still having no finite subcover. The resulting unique path belongs to a covering open set which contains one of its prefix cylinders, contradiction. No arbitrary choice.

references.title: E–W Examples 2.8–2.9 compact metric footnote; elementary binary-tree proof

items.title: Fair-coin cylinder content is a premeasure
items.statement: The fair-coin finitely additive content on the cylinder algebra is a premeasure.
items.strategy: A countable disjoint union in the algebra covering an algebra member is an open cover of a compact clopen set. A finite subcover reduces countable additivity to finite additivity; remaining members are empty.

items.title: Fair-coin measure on binary sequences
items.statement: Assuming countable choice, there is a unique Borel probability on Ω with cylinder masses 2^-k. Its completion is also available.
items.strategy: Apply Caratheodory to the premeasure; prefix cylinders are a countable base, so the generated sigma-algebra is Borel. This is not a general infinite-product theorem.

references.title: E–W Examples 2.8–2.9 with local Caratheodory route

items.title: The fair-coin one-sided shift preserves measure and is mixing
items.statement: The left shift σ(x)_j=x_{j+1} preserves fair-coin measure and is strongly mixing, hence ergodic.
items.strategy: Preimages preserve cylinder masses; widely separated coordinate sets give exactly independent cylinders by finite counting. Apply the generator criterion and mixing implication.

items.title: A countable dense family of continuous functions on a compact metric space
items.statement: Assume countable choice. For nonempty compact metric K, C(K,R) has a countable uniformly dense family.
items.strategy: Choose countable dense {x_j}; distance functions d(·,x_j) separate points. Rational polynomials in finitely many of these and 1 form a countable family. Its real algebra is dense by Stone–Weierstrass; approximate the finite coefficient lists rationally.

references.title: E–W §4.1 pp.97–98, replacing weak-star compactness with the design-required local argument

items.title: Probability sequences on compact metric spaces have integral-convergent subsequences
items.statement: Assume countable choice. Every sequence of Borel probabilities on nonempty compact metric K has a subsequence whose integrals converge for every continuous real f to the integrals of a Borel probability.
items.strategy: Diagonalize bounded integrals on the countable dense family. Uniform estimates extend convergence to all C(K). The limit functional is positive, linear and sends 1 to 1. RMK represents it; compactness makes C_c=C.

references.title: E–W §4.1 pp.97–98; local diagonal/RMK replacement for source weak-star compactness

items.title: Krylov–Bogolyubov existence of an invariant probability
items.statement: Assume countable choice. Every continuous self-map T of a nonempty compact metric space K admits an invariant Borel probability.
items.strategy: Average point masses along one orbit and use the previous subsequence lemma. Telescoping bounds the discrepancy for f∘T and f by 2||f||∞/N. The pushforward is Borel and regular; RMK uniqueness gives equality. Do not invoke Banach–Alaoglu.

items.title: False: measure-preserving transformations are invertible
items.statement: False even on a probability space.
items.strategy: D(0)=D(1/2), so actual invertibility fails. For mod-null invertibility both halves have overlapping image after removal of a null set by scaling; no conull restriction is injective.

items.title: False: ergodicity implies strong mixing
items.statement: False for an irrational circle rotation.
items.strategy: Return subsequence n_j α→0 gives correlation of a half-circle with itself tending to 1/2 instead of 1/4.

items.title: False: weak mixing implies strong mixing
items.statement: There exists a weakly mixing probability-preserving transformation that is not strongly mixing.
items.strategy: FATAL OPEN SUPPLIER (policy-fix-1-b1): retain the missing Chacon theorem as a logical dependency. Its local proof must construct an invertible Lebesgue probability system modulo null sets, prove that all complex L2 eigenfunctions are constant, bridge that property to the absolute-Cesaro definition in def-strong-and-weak-mixing, and exhibit a measurable set whose correlations fail to converge to the product. The prerequisite pairs in batch notes must be inserted before this page in both plan and prose. Neither the later Hilbert/compact-operator pages nor a recorded remark is an earlier proved supplier. No proof or complete transitive closure is certified until these obligations close.

references.title: Katok–Thouvenot, §5.2.3, pp.696–697, Theorem 5.12 (prerequisite proof source; local supplier still absent)

items.title: False: Poincare recurrence needs no finite total measure
items.statement: Translation x↦x+1 on (R,λ) preserves measure but points of [0,1) never return.
items.strategy: Preimages translate sets, whereas positive iterates of [0,1) are disjoint from it.

items.title: False: an ergodic invariant sigma-algebra has only two sets
items.statement: An ergodic system can have nonempty proper strict invariant null sets.
items.strategy: For doubling the dyadic rationals in [0,1) form a nonempty proper null set with D^-1 Q_2=Q_2.

items.title: False: every orbit of an ergodic system is dense
items.statement: Doubling is λ-ergodic but the orbit of zero is {0}.
items.strategy: Zero is fixed and the circle has other points.

items.title: False: constant continuous invariants characterize measure ergodicity
items.statement: A probability-preserving map may have only constant continuous invariant functions and yet fail measure ergodicity.
items.strategy: For D, f∘D=f and the density of preimages of zero force every continuous invariant f constant. Use μ=(δ_0+(δ_{1/3}+δ_{2/3})/2)/2; the invariant set of eventual preimages of 0 has μ=1/2.

references.title: E–W ergodicity definition and doubling example; explicit measure specialization

title: Measure Preserving Transformations and Poincare Recurrence — Examples

items.title: An explicit invariant set for a rational rotation
items.statement: For α=p/q in lowest terms, union_{j=0}^{q-1}[j/q,j/q+1/(2q)) is invariant and has measure 1/2.
items.strategy: Rotation permutes these intervals.

items.title: Dyadic preimages under doubling
items.strategy: Compute both branches. Forward image D[0,1/2)=[0,1) has twice the measure.

items.title: Fair-coin cylinder masses and separated blocks
items.statement: The cylinders [0],[01],[101] have masses 1/2,1/4,1/8; [01] intersect σ^-3[10] has mass 1/16.
items.strategy: Count distinct prescribed coordinates; no probabilistic independence theorem is assumed.

items.title: Recurrence to a dyadic interval under doubling
items.statement: Almost every x in [0,1/4) returns infinitely often to that interval under doubling.
items.strategy: Apply recurrence on the unit-probability circle. No every-point conclusion or return frequency is asserted.

items.title: Kac mean return to a half-circle under irrational rotation
items.statement: For irrational α and E=[0,1/2], ∫_E r_E dλ=1 and the normalized mean is 2.
items.strategy: Apply Kac with λ(E)=1/2. Endpoints change no integral; no assertion that each return time equals two.

items.title: Mod-null invariance need not be strict invariance
items.statement: E={0} is mod-null invariant under D but D^-1 E={0,1/2} differs from E.
items.strategy: Both finite sets are null; calculate the preimage.

items.title: Doubling ergodicity depends on the invariant measure
items.statement: D is ergodic for λ and δ_0, but not for μ=(δ_0+(δ_{1/3}+δ_{2/3})/2)/2.
items.strategy: The two periodic-orbit probabilities are invariant; their mixture assigns mass 1/2 to the strict invariant eventual-zero set. This corrects the design’s false δ_0 counterexample.

references.title: E–W Definition 2.13 and periodic orbit specialization

items.title: Irrational rotation is ergodic but not weakly mixing
items.statement: An irrational rotation is not weakly mixing for λ.
items.strategy: Use f(x)=exp(2πix), whose mean is zero and whose absolute self-correlation at every iterate is one. This is one explicit function computation, not the Fourier-series ergodicity proof.

items.title: Kac normalization needs ergodicity
items.statement: For identity on [0,1] and E=[0,1/2], r_E=1 but ∫_E r_E dλ=1/2.
items.strategy: Compute directly; normalized mean is one, not 1/λ(E).

items.title: The Gauss map preserves Gauss measure
items.statement: On [0,1), define G(0)=0 and G(x)={1/x}. The probability with density 1/(log(2)(1+x)) is invariant.
items.strategy: Use inverse branches x=1/(n+y): transformed densities telescope as sum_{n≥1}1/((n+y)(n+y+1))=1/(1+y). Handle branch endpoints as a countable null set. Ergodicity is deferred, not used.
